extracted.intended_audience: Users and developers of Isabelle (Isabelle/HOL, Isabelle/ZF); theorem-proving practitioners implementing proofs and proof automation
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for using Isabelle's generic tools and packages (Splitter, Simpliﬁer, Classical Reasoner, automated methods, wrappers, object-logic setup, and inductive/coinductive definitions) when developing and automating proofs. Covers when to apply tactics, how to declare rules, how to control search, and debugging/unification options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Case splitting: conclusion vs premises
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a distinction between case splitting in the conclusion and in the premises of a subgoal: splitting in the conclusion is performed by Splitter.split_tac (rules like if_split or option.split) which do not split the subgoal, while splitting in premises is done by Splitter.split_asm_tac (rules like if_split_asm or option.split_asm) which split the subgoal. Splitter.add_split automatically chooses which tactic to call, analysing the form of the rules given as argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case splits should be allowed only when necessary; they are expensive and hard to control. Case-splitting on if-expressions in the conclusion is usually beneficial and is enabled by default in Isabelle/HOL and Isabelle/FOL/ZF. Warning: With Splitter.split_asm_tac as looper component, the Simpliﬁer may split subgoals, possibly causing unexpected problems in tactic expressions that silently assume 0 or 1 subgoals after simplification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simpliﬁed attribute (forward simplification)
rubrics_metrics.description: The simpliﬁed attribute causes a theorem to be simplified, either by exactly the specified rules a1...an or by the implicit Simpliﬁer context; the result is fully simplified by default, including assumptions and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Forward simplification restricts the Simpliﬁer to basic term rewriting; solver and looper tactics are not involved. The simpliﬁed attribute should be only rarely required under normal circumstances. Options like no_asm tune the Simpliﬁer similarly to the simp method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sequent-style reasoning for automation
rubrics_metrics.description: The sequent calculus (Γ ⟹ Δ with multiple conclusions) generalizes natural deduction and is easier to automate; sequent rules are classified as right (introduction-like) or left (elimination-like).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simulate sequents in natural-deduction based Isabelle by representing P1,...,Pm ⟹ Q1,...,Qn as P1 =⇒ ... =⇒ Pm =⇒ ¬Q2 =⇒ ... =⇒ ¬Qn =⇒ Q1, using elim-resolution and swapped introduction rules to operate on right-side formulae. Use sequent-style elimination rules instead of destruction rules for certain connectives; be aware that the simulation affects how (¬L) and other rules behave.

rubrics_metrics.name: Swapped forms for introduction rules when simulating sequents
rubrics_metrics.description: To operate on negated right-side formulae in the sequent simulation, each introduction rule is converted into a swapped form (resolved with the swap principle ¬P =⇒ (¬R =⇒ P) =⇒ R).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: swapped form of (∧I) becomes ¬(P ∧ Q) =⇒ (¬R =⇒ P) =⇒ (¬R =⇒ Q) =⇒ R; the swapped form of (−→I) is ¬(P −→ Q) =⇒ (¬R =⇒ P =⇒ Q) =⇒ R. Swapped introduction rules are applied using elim-resolution, which deletes the negated formula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra sequent rules for classical equivalences and quantifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: Some connectives and quantifier behaviour require dedicated sequent-style rules: e.g. (¬Q =⇒ P) =⇒ P ∨ Q simulates (∨R), and (P −→ Q) =⇒ (¬P =⇒ R) =⇒ (Q =⇒ R) =⇒ R replaces (−→E). Quantifier replication requires special rules to reflect classical dualities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dual rules for quantifiers (∃R and ∀L duality) and consider replication rules (e.g. ∀x.Px =⇒ (Pt =⇒ ∀x.Px =⇒ Q) =⇒ Q) when completeness is needed. Forgoing replication gains decidability by making the search space finite; replication makes the search infinite and must be applied with care.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe vs unsafe rule classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules declared to the Classical Reasoner are classified as introduction, elimination or destruction and as safe or unsafe. In general, safe rules can be attempted blindly, while unsafe rules must be used with care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A safe rule must never reduce a provable goal to an unprovable set of subgoals. Examples of unsafe rules: P =⇒ P ∨ Q (premature choice), any rule whose premises contain new unknowns, ∀x.Px =⇒ (Pt =⇒ Q) =⇒ Q (unsafe because elim-resolution discards ∀x.Px), Pt =⇒ ∃x.Px. The safe/unsafe distinction is fuzzy and used to give priority; any inference that instantiates an unknown shared with other subgoals is unsafe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring rules and attributes for the Classical Reasoner
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands/attributes: intro, elim, dest, rule, iff, swapped; print_claset prints the rule collection. By default rules are unsafe; prefix '!' classifies as safe; '?' marks coincide with Isabelle/Pure declarations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The optional natural number is a weight for single-step rule method ordering (ignored by automated tools). Introduction rules generate swapped forms internally. Rules are sorted by the number of new subgoals they yield (fewer subgoals tried first); later declarations take precedence. rule del deletes a rule regardless of classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of iff declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: iff declares logical equivalences to the Simpliﬁer and the Classical reasoner simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-conditional iff rules result in a safe introduction and elimination pair; conditional ones are considered unsafe. Rules with negative conclusions are automatically inverted. The '?' version of iff declares rules to the Isabelle/Pure context only (omits Simpliﬁer declaration).

rubrics_metrics.name: swapped attribute to turn introduction into elimination
rubrics_metrics.description: swapped turns an introduction rule into an elimination by resolving with the classical swap principle in the second position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is mainly illustrative: the Classical Reasoner already swaps rules internally, but swapped can be used to create explicit elimination forms for demonstration or special use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing structured methods: rule and contradiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical version of rule observes the classical rule context in addition to Isabelle/Pure. contradiction solves a goal by deriving A and ¬A; chained facts may appear in either order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the classical rule method when you need the classical rule context. Use contradiction when a goal can be closed by contradiction; it will locate and use chained facts as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick fully-automated method based on goal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully automated methods include blast (separate classical tableau prover), auto (combines classical reasoning with simplification), force (exhaustive proof for first subgoal), fast/best/slow (sequent-style searches with different search strategies), fastforce/slowsimp/bestsimp (variants with Simpliﬁer), and deepen (exhaustive search up to limited depth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: blast is faster/powerful but has limitations (no classical wrapper tacticals, no higher-order unification, function-variable restrictions); it can take an optional bound for unsafe steps. auto is good for many mostly-trivial subgoals; force is exhaustive but can be long or diverge; fast uses depth-first, best uses best-first guided by heuristics (proof-state size), slow does broader search and may undo assumption-proofs on backtracking. Use the *_simp or *_force variants when integration with the Simpliﬁer is needed. If blast runs slowly, try fast or other tools, or supply an explicit search bound (blast lim) when a successful bound is known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deepen for exhaustive depth-bounded search
rubrics_metrics.description: deepen performs exhaustive search up to a certain depth (start depth 4, increased iteratively up to 10), modifying unsafe rules to preserve the formula they act on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: deepen can prove more goals than fast but is much slower, especially when assumptions have many universal quantifiers. Use deepen when deeper exhaustive search is required and you can tolerate long runtimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partially automated methods for simplifying hard goals
rubrics_metrics.description: safe repeatedly performs safe steps deterministically; clarify performs safe steps without splitting subgoals; clarsimp acts like clarify but also does simplification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use safe when you want deterministic safe-step transformation. Use clarify when you want to avoid splitting (e.g., leave A ∧ B as a conjunction). clarsimp is useful to combine safe steps and simplifier, but may still split if the Simpliﬁer context includes a splitter for premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-step tactics for fine control
rubrics_metrics.description: Primitive tactics: safe_step (safe step on first subgoal, no instantiation), inst_step (allows unknown instantiation), step (basic step applying unsafe wrapper tacticals and rules), slow_step (allows backtracking between instantiation and unsafe rules), clarify_step (safe step without splitting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Call these primitives to execute the classical reasoner procedures one step at a time when fully/partially automated methods fail or when interactive control is needed. safe_step applies safe wrapper tacticals and avoids instantiating unknowns; inst_step is like safe_step but permits instantiation; step may apply unsafe rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modify proof search with safe/unsafe wrappers and simpset integration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Classical Reasoner applies two lists of wrapper tacticals (safe wrappers affect safe_step; unsafe wrappers affect step/slow_step). Wrappers transform each search step by attempting tactics before/after the original step tactic. Functions: addSWrapper/addSbefore/addSafter/delSWrapper for safe wrappers; addWrapper/addbefore/addafter/delWrapper for unsafe wrappers. addSss/addss add the context simpset to the classical set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initially wrapper lists are empty. Use ctxt addSbefore/addSafter to try tactics before/after safe steps, and addbefore/addafter for unsafe steps. del* deletes wrappers. addSss causes the assumptions and goal to be simplified after each safe step; addss simplifies before each unsafe step. Use wrappers sparingly to customize search behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-logic setup: judgment, atomize, and rule_format
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare a truth judgment for the object-logic using judgment; atomize (method/attribute) rewrites non-atomic premises using meta-level equations to make nested goals amenable to resolution; rule_format (attribute) rewrites a theorem by rulify equalities, normalizing ∀ and −→ into rule statements over meta-level connectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only atomize (method) and rule_format are occasionally required by end-users; other commands are for writing object-logics. Use atomize (with (full) option if desired) to internalize nested object-level constructs for automated reasoning (important for locales). Use rule_format to get rules in a form suitable for the Classical Reasoner and Simpliﬁer (no_asm restricts to conclusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracing and bounds for higher-order uniﬁcation
rubrics_metrics.description: Tracing options: unify_trace, unify_trace_simp, unify_trace_types control printing of unification tracing; unify_trace_bound controls when tracing prints (depth threshold); unify_search_bound bounds unification search depth. These options are global (not local to a context).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable tracing to diagnose higher-order unification problems; unify_search_bound prevents unification from searching past the given depth (avoids infinite/infeasible searches) but may cut off solutions and cause a "Uniﬁcation bound exceeded" warning. Default bounds are high; adjust only when necessary for debugging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive and coinductive definitions: monotonicity and declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: inductive / coinductive define the least / greatest predicate or set closed under provided introduction rules; the optional monos declaration contains monotonicity theorems required for operators applied to recursive sets. for fixes lists parameters fixed across the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monotonicity of recursion schemes must be proven as a prerequisite: provide or rely on existing monotonicity lemmas (default Isabelle/HOL declarations handle common cases). Use inductive_set / coinductive_set for native HOL predicates simulating multiple arguments by tuples. print_inductives prints definitions and monotonicity rules; use the '!' option for extra verbosity. Derived theorems include R.intros, R.cases, and R.induct/R.coinduct.
